{{Short description|Axiom of probability theory}}
{{Distinguish|Unit of measurement}}
'''Unit measure''' is an [[Probability axioms|axiom]] of [[probability theory]]<ref>A. Kolmogorov, "Foundations of the theory of probability" 1933. English translation by Nathan Morrison 1956 copyright Chelsea Publishing Company.</ref> that states that the [[probability]] of the entire [[sample space]] is equal to one ([[1 (number)|unity]]); that is, ''P''(''S'')=1 where ''S'' is the sample space. Loosely speaking, it means that ''S'' must be chosen so that when the experiment is performed, ''something'' happens. The term ''measure'' here refers to the [[measure theory|measure-theoretic]] approach to probability.

Violations of unit measure have been reported in arguments about the outcomes of events<ref>R. Christensen and T. Reichert: "Unit measure violations in pattern recognition: ambiguity and irrelevancy" Pattern Recognition, 8, No. 4 1976.</ref><ref>T. Oldberg and R. Christensen "Erratic measure" NDE for the Energy Industry 1995, American Society of Mechanical Engineers, New York, NY.</ref> under which events acquire "probabilities" that are not the probabilities of probability theory. In situations such as these the term "probability" serves as a false premise to the associated argument.
